newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian press says Vranitzky exits on cue.
newsitem.headline: Austrian press says Vranitzky exits on cue.

text.p: Austrian newspapers said on Sunday Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's decision to resign after more than a decade in power was well timed and praised the political talents of designated successor Viktor Klima.

Vranitzky, Europe's second longest-serving leader after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, announced on Saturday he was stepping down and named Finance Minister Klima as his successor as chancellor and Social Democratic Party leader.
"Klima follows Vranitzky: The Social Democrats set about rebuilding their fortunes," wrote the daily Kurier in an editorial, forecasting a wide-ranging reshuffle of the Social Democrat team.
Klima, 49, was cast from the same mould as his predecessor but had greater determination and was more adept at winning opponents round, the paper said.
"Klima represents continuity but with different means. He is cleverer, more capable of getting the desired results and has a better instinct for power," Kurier said.

The chancellor-designate could face his first challenge within days. The conservative People's Party, which governs in coalition with the Social Democrats, has insisted it wants a say in the appointment of a new finance minister.

"We want to make our thoughts known and we do not want to find out via the media," said People's Party leader Wolfgang Schuessel, apparently smarting from Vranitzky's failure to inform him in advance of his resignation.
Social Democrat parliamentary speaker Heinz Fischer swiftly dismissed Schuessel's demands.
"That is not in the coalition agreement," he said.
Klima appeared to have gone underground, keeping out of the media spotlight and maintaining silence on his future plans.
Columnists agreed that Vranitzky's decision to go was the right one in personal and political terms.

"Shortly before he announced his resignation, the chancellor appeared relaxed and cheerful. One sensed this was a step he had considered long and hard," said tabloid Neue Kronen Zeitung, Austria's biggest circulation daily.

Vranitzky, acclaimed for leading his country into the European Union and apologising to Jews for Austria's part in the Nazi Holocaust, had suffered waning popularity at home even as his profile abroad strengthened.

But the softly spoken former banker said his going had nothing to do with his party's abysmal results in last October's European Parliament elections nor with any strife within the coalition. He said it was just time to go.
"I thought that, after so many years, it would be a wise decision to transfer responsibility to younger people in the party," he told reporters after announcing his resignation.

Kurier pointed out that Vranitzky's party had largely recovered from its humiliation in the European vote, winning a battle of wills with the People's Party over the sale of flagship bank, Creditanstalt.
The Social Democrats' Fischer reinforced that view: "(Vranitzky) just believed it was better for the country and this point in time was optimal."

Nationalist Freedom Party leader Joerg Haider, whose extreme rightwing party is the nation's third political force, was less flattering, accusing Vranitzky of ruining the Social Democrats and alienating working class voters.
"My prophecy that I would still be working for Austria while he would be long gone has come true," said Haider, who also predicts he will be chancellor by the turn of the century.
